nodes.by: Named after separate publications by Tibor Gallai, Maria Hasse, B. Roy and L. M. Vitaver; Roy credits the statement to a conjecture in a 1958 graph theory textbook by Claude Berge
nodes.note: It generalizes Rédei's 1934 theorem that every tournament contains a directed Hamiltonian path.

nodes.name: Berge's theorem
nodes.statement: A matching M in a graph G has the largest possible number of edges if and only if there is no augmenting path with respect to M. An augmenting path starts and ends on unmatched vertices and alternates between edges in M and edges not in M.
nodes.by: Claude Berge, 1957; already observed by Petersen in 1891 and Kőnig in 1931

nodes.name: Glaisher's theorem
nodes.statement: For every positive integer d and every positive integer n, the number of partitions of n into parts not divisible by d equals the number of partitions of n in which no part is repeated d or more times.
nodes.by: James Whitbread Lee Glaisher, 1883; the case d = 2 was established by Leonhard Euler, 1748
nodes.note: For d = 2 it becomes Euler's theorem: the number of partitions of n into distinct parts equals the number of partitions of n into odd parts.

nodes.name: Graph structure theorem
nodes.statement: For any graph H there is a positive integer k such that every graph without H as a minor can be built as follows. Start with a list of graphs, each embedded on a surface on which H does not embed; add to each at most k vortices of depth at most k; add to each at most k new vertices (apices) with any number of edges having at least one endpoint among the apices; finally join the resulting graphs by k-clique-sums.
nodes.by: Neil Robertson and Paul Seymour, stated in the seventeenth of their series of 23 papers
nodes.note: It implies that for every planar graph H, the graphs without H as a minor have bounded tree width. Its proof is very long and involved.

nodes.name: Grinberg's theorem
nodes.statement: Let G be a finite planar graph, drawn in the plane without crossings, that has a Hamiltonian cycle C (a cycle passing through every vertex exactly once). If f_k and g_k are the numbers of faces with k sides inside and outside C, then ∑ over k ≥ 3 of (k − 2)(f_k − g_k) = 0.
nodes.by: Emanuel Grinberg, 1968
nodes.note: It is a necessary condition for a planar graph to be Hamiltonian, so a graph that fails it is not Hamiltonian. It has been used to show that some counterexamples to Tait's conjecture are not Hamiltonian.

nodes.name: Grötzsch's theorem
nodes.statement: Every triangle-free planar graph can be colored with three colors, so that the two endpoints of every edge have different colors.
nodes.by: Herbert Grötzsch, 1959
nodes.note: The four-color theorem says four colors suffice for every planar graph. Grötzsch's theorem says three suffice when the graph has no three mutually adjacent vertices.

nodes.name: Halin's grid theorem
nodes.statement: An infinite graph has a thick end exactly when it contains a subdivision of the hexagonal tiling of the plane. A thick end is an end that contains infinitely many pairwise disjoint rays.
nodes.by: Rudolf Halin, 1965
nodes.note: It is a precursor to the work of Robertson and Seymour linking treewidth to large grid minors in finite graphs.

nodes.name: Halpern–Läuchli theorem
nodes.statement: Let d and r be natural numbers and T₀, …, T_{d−1} finitely splitting trees of height ω, and colour each tuple made of one node from each tree, all on the same level, with one of r colours. Then there are subtrees Sᵢ strongly embedded in the Tᵢ such that all such same-level tuples from the Sᵢ have the same colour.
nodes.by: Halpern–Läuchli–Laver–Pincus (James D. Halpern, Hans Läuchli, Richard Laver and David Pincus), following Milliken (1979)
nodes.note: Its original purpose was to give a model for set theory in which the Boolean prime ideal theorem is true but the axiom of choice is false.

nodes.name: Hobby–Rice theorem
nodes.statement: For any n continuously integrable functions g₁, …, gₙ from [0,1] to ℝ, there is a division of [0,1] into n+1 subintervals by n points, with each subinterval given a sign +1 or −1, such that for each of the n functions the signed sum of its integrals over the subintervals is 0. In other words, each function has the same integral over the positive subintervals as over the negative ones.
nodes.by: Charles R. Hobby and John R. Rice, 1965; simplified proof by A. Pinkus, 1976
nodes.note: Noga Alon used it for necklace splitting in 1987. It implies that a cake can be cut with n cuts into two parts that all n partners value equally.

nodes.name: Max-flow min-cut theorem
nodes.statement: In a network given by a finite directed graph with a source, a sink and a nonnegative real capacity on each edge, the maximum value of a flow from the source to the sink equals the minimum capacity of a cut. A cut splits the vertices into a part containing the source and a part containing the sink, and its capacity is the total capacity of the edges leading from the source part to the sink part.
nodes.by: Ford and Fulkerson, soon after the problem was posed to them by T. E. Harris in 1955
nodes.note: It is a special case of the duality theorem for linear programs and can be used to derive Menger's theorem and the Kőnig–Egerváry theorem.

nodes.name: Isolation lemma of Mulmuley, Vazirani and Vazirani
nodes.statement: Let n and N be positive integers and F any nonempty family of subsets of {1, …, n}. If each element of {1, …, n} gets an integer weight chosen independently and uniformly at random from {1, …, N}, and the weight of a set is the sum of the weights of its elements, then with probability at least 1 − n/N exactly one set in F has the minimum weight.
nodes.by: Mulmuley, Vazirani and Vazirani, 1987
nodes.note: It can be used to obtain a randomized parallel algorithm for the maximum matching problem, and it gives a simpler proof of the Valiant–Vazirani theorem.

nodes.name: Knaster–Tarski theorem
nodes.statement: Let (L, ≤) be a complete lattice and let f : L → L be an order-preserving (monotonic) function with respect to ≤. Then the set of fixed points of f in L forms a complete lattice under ≤.
nodes.by: Named after Bronisław Knaster and Alfred Tarski; Tarski stated it in its most general form, and earlier Knaster and Tarski established the case where L is the lattice of subsets of a set
nodes.note: In particular f has a least and a greatest fixed point. The theorem is used in the semantics of programming languages, abstract interpretation and game theory.

nodes.name: Multinomial theorem
nodes.statement: For any positive integer m and any non-negative integer n, (x₁ + x₂ + ⋯ + x_m)ⁿ equals the sum, over all choices of non-negative integers k₁, …, k_m with k₁ + ⋯ + k_m = n, of n!/(k₁! k₂! ⋯ k_m!) · x₁^k₁ · x₂^k₂ ⋯ x_m^k_m.
nodes.note: It generalizes the binomial theorem, which is the case m = 2. Setting every xᵢ = 1 shows that the multinomial coefficients for given n and m add up to mⁿ.

nodes.name: Behrend's theorem
nodes.statement: Call a subset of {1, …, n} primitive if none of its elements is a multiple of another. Its logarithmic density is the sum of 1/i over its elements i, divided by 1 + 1/2 + ⋯ + 1/n (equivalently, by log n). Every primitive subset has logarithmic density O(1/√(log log n)), and for infinite primitive sequences the density is o(1/√(log log n)).
nodes.by: Felix Behrend, proved 1934 and published 1935; Paul Erdős independently proved the same result in 1934
nodes.note: The set of numbers with exactly k prime factors, for k about log log n, has logarithmic density (1+o(1))/√(2π log log n), so the bound has the best possible form.

nodes.name: Conway's 99-graph problem
nodes.statement: The problem asks whether there is an undirected graph with 99 vertices in which every two adjacent vertices have exactly one common neighbor and every two non-adjacent vertices have exactly two common neighbors. Equivalently, every edge lies in a unique triangle and every non-adjacent pair is one of the two diagonals of a unique 4-cycle.
nodes.by: Possibility suggested by Norman L. Biggs, 1969; John Horton Conway offered a $1000 prize for its solution in 2014
nodes.note: Such a graph would have to be a strongly regular graph with parameters (99,14,1,2). It cannot have symmetries that take every vertex to every other vertex.

nodes.name: Kawasaki's theorem
nodes.statement: A crease pattern on a flat sheet of paper, with 2n creases all starting from one vertex inside the sheet and consecutive angles α₁, α₂, …, α₂ₙ between them, can be folded flat with every crease folded and no other folds if and only if α₁ − α₂ + α₃ − … − α₂ₙ = 0, which is the same as each of the two alternating sets of angles summing to 180 degrees. A pattern with an odd number of creases never folds flat.
nodes.by: Discovered independently by Toshikazu Kawasaki, Stuart Robertson and Jacques Justin in the late 1970s and early 1980s; sufficiency of the condition may first have been stated by Hull (1994)
nodes.note: Crease patterns with more than one vertex do not obey such a simple criterion and are NP-hard to fold. The theorem is also called the Kawasaki–Justin theorem or Husimi's theorem.

nodes.name: Labelled enumeration theorem
nodes.statement: Suppose labelled objects, none of size zero, are given by an exponential generating function g(z), and one object is placed in each of n slots that are permuted by a permutation group G. Then the exponential generating function of the number of different configurations under the re-labelling process is fₙ(z) = g(z)ⁿ/|G|. If G is the symmetric group on the n slots, then the sum over n of fₙ(z)tⁿ equals e^{g(z)t}.
nodes.note: It is the labelled counterpart of the Pólya enumeration theorem.

nodes.name: Lambek–Moser theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be a non-decreasing, unbounded function from positive integers to non-negative integers, and let f*(n) be the number of values x with f(x) < n. Then every positive integer occurs exactly once among the values of F(n) = f(n) + n and F*(n) = f*(n) + n, and F and F* list the two complementary sets in increasing order. Conversely, every partition of the positive integers into two infinite complementary sets arises in this way.
nodes.by: Joachim Lambek and Leo Moser, 1954
nodes.note: When a formula is known for the nth number in a set, the theorem can give a formula for the nth number not in the set. It extends Rayleigh's theorem on complementary Beatty sequences.

nodes.name: Nash-Williams theorem
nodes.statement: A graph G has t edge-disjoint spanning trees if and only if, for every partition of its vertices into k non-empty parts, at least t(k − 1) edges join vertices in different parts.
nodes.by: Proved independently by Tutte and Nash-Williams, 1961; Kaiser gave a short elementary proof in 2012
nodes.note: In 1964 Nash-Williams generalized it to partitions of a graph into edge-disjoint forests. As a corollary, every 2k-edge connected graph has k edge-disjoint spanning trees.

nodes.name: Rural hospitals theorem
nodes.statement: Suppose finitely many doctors are matched to finitely many hospitals, each doctor to at most one hospital and each hospital having several positions, and all preferences of doctors and hospitals are strict. Then the set of assigned doctors and the number of filled positions in each hospital are the same in all stable matchings, and any hospital with an empty position in some stable matching receives exactly the same set of doctors in all stable matchings.
nodes.by: Special case with one position per hospital proved by McVitie and Wilson, 1970; the two parts of the full theorem proved by Alvin E. Roth in the 1980s
nodes.note: It shows that changing the matching mechanism, as long as it produces stable matchings, does not help rural hospitals: they receive neither more doctors nor better doctors.

nodes.name: Levi's lemma
nodes.statement: For all strings u, v, x and y, if uv = xy, then there is a string w such that either uw = x and v = wy (when |u| ≤ |x|), or u = xw and wv = y (when |u| ≥ |x|).
nodes.by: Friedrich Wilhelm Levi, 1944
nodes.note: A monoid in which Levi's lemma holds is said to have the equidivisibility property.

nodes.name: Lindström–Gessel–Viennot lemma
nodes.statement: Let G be a locally finite directed acyclic graph with edge weights in a commutative ring, and let a₁,…,aₙ and b₁,…,bₙ be vertices such that for i < j and k < l every path from aᵢ to b_l meets every path from aⱼ to b_k. Let e(a, b) be the sum of the weights of all paths from a to b, and M the matrix with entries e(aᵢ, bⱼ). Then det(M) is the sum, over all n-tuples of pairwise vertex-disjoint paths with Pᵢ going from aᵢ to b_σ(i) for some permutation σ, of sign(σ) times the product of the weights of the paths. With all weights 1 and only the identity permutation possible, det(M) is the number of such non-intersecting n-tuples.
nodes.by: Gessel and Viennot, 1985, based on earlier work of Lindström, 1973
nodes.note: It gives a way to count tuples of non-intersecting lattice paths, or more generally paths on a directed graph.

nodes.name: MacMahon's master theorem
nodes.statement: Let A = (a_ij) be an m×m complex matrix and x₁,…,x_m formal variables. For nonnegative integers k₁,…,k_m, let G(k₁,…,k_m) be the coefficient of x₁^k₁⋯x_m^k_m in the product over i of (∑_j a_ij x_j)^k_i. Let t₁,…,t_m be further formal variables and T the diagonal matrix diag(t₁,…,t_m). Then the sum of G(k₁,…,k_m) t₁^k₁⋯t_m^k_m over all nonnegative integer vectors (k₁,…,k_m) equals 1/det(I − TA), where I is the m×m identity matrix.
nodes.by: Percy MacMahon, 1916
nodes.note: It is often used to derive binomial identities, most notably Dixon's identity.

nodes.name: Milliken's tree theorem
nodes.statement: Let T be a finitely splitting rooted tree of height ω and n a positive integer. If the collection of all strongly embedded subtrees of T of height n is split into finitely many classes, then there is a strongly embedded infinite subtree R of T such that all strongly embedded subtrees of R of height n lie in one class.
nodes.by: Keith R. Milliken, 1979
nodes.note: It generalizes Ramsey's theorem to infinite trees, and it implies Ramsey's theorem when T is taken to be a linear ordering on ω vertices.

nodes.name: Milliken–Taylor theorem
nodes.statement: Colour the k-element subsets of ℕ with finitely many colours. Then there is a sequence a₀, a₁, a₂, … in ℕ such that all k-element sets {sum of a_t over t in α₁, …, sum of a_t over t in αₖ} have the same colour, where α₁, …, αₖ are finite sets of indices with each set lying entirely below the next.
nodes.by: Named after Keith Milliken and Alan D. Taylor
nodes.note: It generalizes both Ramsey's theorem and Hindman's theorem.

nodes.name: Mirsky's theorem
nodes.statement: For every finite partially ordered set, the height (the largest number of elements in a chain, a subset in which every two elements are comparable) equals the smallest number of antichains (subsets in which no two elements are comparable) into which the set can be partitioned.
nodes.by: Mirsky, 1971
nodes.note: It is closely related to Dilworth's theorem and the Erdős–Szekeres theorem. It extends immediately to infinite partially ordered sets of finite height.

nodes.name: Mnëv's universality theorem
nodes.statement: Let V be a semialgebraic variety in ℝⁿ defined over the integers. Then V is stably equivalent to the realization space of some oriented matroid, that is, to the space of all point configurations that induce one fixed oriented matroid.
nodes.by: Nikolai Mnëv, 1986
nodes.note: Informally, point configurations of a fixed combinatorics can show arbitrarily complicated behavior. It also gives the universality theorem for convex polytopes.

nodes.name: New digraph reconstruction conjecture
nodes.statement: If D and E are any two digraphs and f is a bijection from V(D) to V(E) such that, for every vertex v of D, the digraphs D∖{v} and E∖{f(v)} (with that vertex deleted) are isomorphic and v and f(v) have the same outdegree and the same indegree, then D and E are isomorphic.
nodes.by: Ramachandran, 1979
nodes.note: It is stronger than Ulam's reconstruction conjecture but weaker than the disproved digraph reconstruction conjecture. It is also known as the degree associated reconstruction conjecture, and as of 2026 no counterexample is known.

nodes.name: Petersen's theorem
nodes.statement: Every cubic, bridgeless graph contains a perfect matching. That is, if a graph has exactly three edges at each vertex and every edge belongs to a cycle, then it has a set of edges that touches every vertex exactly once.
nodes.by: Julius Petersen, 1891; simplified proofs by Frink (1926) and König (1936)
nodes.note: It is one of the earliest results in graph theory. Modern textbooks cover it as an application of Tutte's theorem on perfect matchings.

nodes.name: Erdős–Ko–Rado theorem
nodes.statement: Let 𝒜 be a family of distinct r-element subsets of an n-element set, with n ≥ 2r, such that every two subsets share at least one element. Then 𝒜 has at most C(n−1, r−1) members. For n > 2r the largest such families are exactly those made of all r-element subsets containing one chosen element.
nodes.by: Paul Erdős, Chao Ko and Richard Rado, proved 1938, published 1961
nodes.note: It can also be stated as the independence number of the Kneser graph KG(n,r) being C(n−1, r−1) for n ≥ 2r.

nodes.name: Planar separator theorem
nodes.statement: In any planar graph with n vertices, the vertices can be split into three sets A, S and B so that A and B each have at most 2n/3 vertices, S has at most a constant times √n vertices (O(√n)), and no edge joins a vertex of A to a vertex of B.
nodes.by: Lipton and Tarjan, 1979; a weaker form with a larger separator was proven by Ungar, 1951
nodes.note: It is a form of isoperimetric inequality for planar graphs. Repeated use of it gives separator hierarchies, which are used to design efficient divide and conquer algorithms for planar graphs.

nodes.name: Szemerédi–Trotter theorem
nodes.statement: Given n points and m lines in the Euclidean plane, the number of incidences, meaning pairs of a point and a line through it, is at most a constant times n^(2/3) m^(2/3) + n + m. This bound cannot be improved except in the constant.
nodes.by: Endre Szemerédi and William T. Trotter; a simpler proof was later found by László Székely
nodes.note: An equivalent form says that for n points and an integer k ≥ 2, the number of lines through at least k of the points is O(n²/k³ + n/k). Consequences include Beck's theorem in incidence geometry.

nodes.name: q-Vandermonde identity
nodes.statement: For q-binomial coefficients, [m+n choose k]_q = ∑ over j of [m choose k−j]_q · [n choose j]_q · q^(j(m−k+j)). The only nonzero terms come from the j with max(0, k−m) ≤ j ≤ min(n, k).
nodes.note: It is a q-analogue of the Chu–Vandermonde identity and can be proved with the q-binomial theorem.

nodes.name: Sperner's lemma
nodes.statement: Divide an n-dimensional simplex with corners A₁, …, A₍ₙ₊₁₎ into smaller n-dimensional simplices that meet face to face. Color each vertex of the division with one of the colors 1, …, n+1 so that each corner Aᵢ gets color i and every vertex on a face spanned by some of the corners gets one of those corners' colors. Then the number of small simplices whose vertices carry all n+1 colors is odd, so there is at least one.
nodes.by: Emanuel Sperner
nodes.note: It is a discrete analogue of the Brouwer fixed point theorem and is equivalent to it. In one dimension it is a discrete version of the intermediate value theorem. Sperner colorings are used to compute fixed points and in fair division (cake cutting) algorithms.

nodes.name: Robbins' theorem
nodes.statement: The edges of an undirected graph G can each be given a direction so that the resulting directed graph has a path from every vertex to every other vertex if and only if G is connected and has no bridge. A bridge is an edge whose removal disconnects the graph.
nodes.by: Robbins, 1939
nodes.note: Equivalently, the graphs with strong orientations are exactly the 2-edge-connected graphs. Robbins proved it using ear decomposition, a tool he introduced for this task, and was motivated by the design of one-way streets in cities.

nodes.name: Rogers–Ramanujan identities
nodes.statement: With (a;q)ₙ the q-Pochhammer symbol, ∑ over n ≥ 0 of q^(n²)/(q;q)ₙ = 1/((q;q⁵)_∞ (q⁴;q⁵)_∞), and ∑ over n ≥ 0 of q^(n²+n)/(q;q)ₙ = 1/((q²;q⁵)_∞ (q³;q⁵)_∞).
nodes.by: Discovered and proved by Rogers, 1894; rediscovered without proof by Srinivasa Ramanujan before 1913; independently rediscovered and proved by Schur, 1917; joint new proof by Rogers and Ramanujan, 1919
nodes.note: In terms of partitions, the number of ways to write n as a sum of parts that differ pairwise by at least 2 equals the number of ways to write n as a sum of parts that are 1 or 4 modulo 5. The second identity gives the same with smallest part at least 2 on one side and parts 2 or 3 modulo 5 on the other.

nodes.name: Rothe–Hagen identity
nodes.statement: For every non-negative integer n and all complex numbers x, y, z for which no denominator vanishes, ∑ₖ₌₀ⁿ [x/(x+kz)]·C(x+kz, k)·[y/(y+(n−k)z)]·C(y+(n−k)z, n−k) = [(x+y)/(x+y+nz)]·C(x+y+nz, n). Here C(a, k) = a(a−1)⋯(a−k+1)/k! is the binomial coefficient.
nodes.by: Heinrich August Rothe, 1793, and Johann Georg Hagen, 1891, independently
nodes.note: It is a generalization of Vandermonde's identity.

nodes.name: Scheinerman's conjecture
nodes.statement: Every planar graph is the intersection graph of a set of line segments in the plane. That is, each vertex can be drawn as a straight line segment so that two vertices are joined by an edge exactly when their segments intersect.
nodes.by: Formulated by E. R. Scheinerman in his Ph.D. thesis, 1984; proved by Chalopin and Gonçalves, 2009
nodes.note: Earlier results had shown that every planar graph is the intersection graph of simple curves in the plane. A related conjecture that four segment directions always suffice was shown false by Gonçalves in 2020.

nodes.name: Schnyder's theorem
nodes.statement: A graph G is planar if and only if the order dimension of its incidence poset P(G) is at most three. The incidence poset has the vertices and edges of G as elements, with a vertex below an edge when it is an endpoint of that edge.
nodes.by: Walter Schnyder, 1989
nodes.note: The order dimension of a partial order is the smallest number of total orderings whose intersection is that partial order. Trotter extended the result to vertices, edges and faces of a convex polyhedron or embedded planar graph, where the dimension is at most four.

nodes.name: Schuette–Nesbitt formula
nodes.statement: Let A_1, …, A_m be subsets of a set Ω; for a point ω let N(ω) be the number of these sets containing ω, and N_k(ω) the number of ways to pick k of the sets so that ω lies in all of them (N_0 = 1). Then for every c_0, …, c_m in a vector space over a field (or a module over a ring with identity), c_{N(ω)} = ∑_{k=0}^{m} N_k(ω) ∑_{l=0}^{k} (−1)^{k−l} C(k,l) c_l at every ω, where C(k,l) is a binomial coefficient; in polynomial form, ∑_{n=0}^{m} 1_{N=n} xⁿ = ∑_{k=0}^{m} N_k (x − 1)^k.
nodes.by: Donald R. Schuette and Cecil J. Nesbitt, 1959 (for independent events); named and generalized to arbitrary events by Hans U. Gerber, 1979; elementary combinatorial proof by Christian Buchta, 1994
nodes.note: It generalizes the inclusion–exclusion principle. Its probabilistic version, with expectations of N_k, is used in actuarial science to calculate the net single premium for life annuities and life insurances.

nodes.name: Stanley's reciprocity theorem
nodes.statement: Let C be a d-dimensional rational cone in ℝᵈ (the points satisfying finitely many homogeneous linear inequalities with integer coefficients), and let F_C(x₁, …, x_d) be the sum of x₁^a₁ ⋯ x_d^a_d over all integer points (a₁, …, a_d) in C, with F_int(C) defined in the same way for the interior of C. Then, as rational functions, F_C(1/x₁, …, 1/x_d) = (−1)ᵈ F_int(C)(x₁, …, x_d).
nodes.by: Named after Richard P. Stanley
nodes.note: It generalizes Ehrhart–Macdonald reciprocity for Ehrhart polynomials of rational convex polytopes. Stanley also coined the term combinatorial reciprocity theorem.

nodes.name: Stanley–Wilf conjecture
nodes.statement: For every permutation β there is a constant C, depending on β, such that the number of permutations of length n that avoid β as a permutation pattern is at most Cⁿ for every n.
nodes.by: Formulated independently by Richard P. Stanley and Herbert Wilf in the late 1980s; proved by Adam Marcus and Gábor Tardos, 2004
nodes.note: Marcus and Tardos actually proved a different conjecture of Füredi and Hajnal (1992), which Klazar had shown in 2000 to imply this one. It is equivalent to the convergence of the n-th root of the number of such permutations as n grows.

nodes.name: Steinitz's theorem
nodes.statement: A finite simple graph is the graph of vertices and edges of a three-dimensional convex polyhedron if and only if it is planar and 3-vertex-connected.
nodes.by: Ernst Steinitz, written 1916 and published 1922; graph-theoretic formulation introduced by Branko Grünbaum and Theodore Motzkin in the early 1960s
nodes.note: It gives a purely combinatorial classification of three-dimensional convex polyhedra, which is not known in higher dimensions.

nodes.name: Symmetric hypergraph theorem
nodes.statement: Let H be a symmetric hypergraph, meaning its automorphism group acts transitively on the vertex set S, and let m = |S|. Then the chromatic number satisfies χ(H) ≤ 1 + (ln m) / (−ln(1 − α(H)/m)), where α(H) is the independence number of H.
nodes.note: Its original reference is unknown and it has been called folklore. It is used in graph Ramsey theory and for colorings that avoid monochromatic arithmetic progressions.

nodes.name: Szymanski's conjecture
nodes.statement: Every permutation σ on the n-dimensional doubly directed hypercube graph can be routed with edge-disjoint paths: for each vertex v there is a path from v to σ(v) such that no two paths use the same edge in the same direction.
nodes.by: Named after Ted H. Szymanski
nodes.note: Computer experiments have verified it for n ≤ 4. For n ≥ 5 it remains open, and there are permutations that need paths which are not shortest paths.

nodes.name: Entropy influence conjecture
nodes.statement: There is an absolute constant C such that for every function f from {−1,1}ⁿ to {−1,1}, H(f) ≤ C·I(f). Here f(x) = ∑ f̂(S) x_S is the Fourier expansion of f, the total influence is I(f) = ∑ |S| f̂(S)², and the entropy of the spectrum is H(f) = −∑ f̂(S)² log f̂(S)², with x log x taken to be 0 when x = 0.
nodes.by: Ehud Friedgut and Gil Kalai, 1996

nodes.name: Topkis's theorem
nodes.statement: Let D be a lattice, and let f(x,θ) be supermodular in x and have increasing differences in (x,θ). Whenever the set of maximizers x*(θ) of f(x,θ) over x in D is nonempty, it is increasing in θ as a correspondence, in the strong set order. Under standard existence conditions, the greatest and least selections from it are nondecreasing in θ.
nodes.by: Named after Donald M. Topkis
nodes.note: It is used to establish comparative statics, including when the objective function is not differentiable.

nodes.name: Tucker's lemma
nodes.statement: Let T be a triangulation of the closed n-dimensional ball whose part on the boundary sphere is antipodally symmetric, so that if σ is a boundary simplex then so is −σ. If every vertex v of T gets a label L(v) from +1, −1, +2, −2, …, +n, −n such that L(−v) = −L(v) for every vertex v on the boundary sphere, then T contains a complementary edge: an edge whose two vertices carry the same number with opposite signs.
nodes.by: Named after Albert W. Tucker
nodes.note: It is a combinatorial analog of the Borsuk–Ulam theorem. Constructive proofs give algorithms that find the complementary edge, and finding it is PPA-complete even for n = 2.

nodes.name: Tutte homotopy theorem
nodes.statement: In a matroid, call any union of circuits a flat: circuits are 0-flats, the minimal nonempty flats that are not 0-flats are 1-flats, and so on, and a path is a finite sequence of circuits in which any two consecutive ones lie in a common 1-flat. Then every closed path can be turned into the trivial path by repeatedly inserting or removing elementary paths, which have the form (X, Y, X) or (X, Y, Z, X) with X, Y, Z in a common 2-flat.
nodes.by: Tutte, 1958
nodes.note: It generalises the idea of a path from graphs to matroids. Flats here are in Tutte's original sense, which differs from modern usage, and a stronger form covers paths that avoid certain convex subsets.

nodes.name: Tutte–Berge formula
nodes.statement: For a graph G = (V, E), the size of a maximum matching equals ½ · min over all subsets U of V of (|U| − odd(G−U) + |V|), where odd(H) is the number of connected components of H with an odd number of vertices. Equivalently, the number of unmatched vertices in a maximum matching equals the maximum over U ⊆ V of (odd(G−U) − |U|).
nodes.by: Claude Berge, who proved it as a generalization of Tutte's theorem; also named after W. T. Tutte
nodes.note: It generalizes Tutte's theorem on perfect matchings, which follows from it as a corollary.

nodes.name: Tverberg's theorem
nodes.statement: For any positive integers d and r, any set of (d + 1)(r − 1) + 1 points in d-dimensional Euclidean space can be partitioned into r subsets whose convex hulls all have a common point.
nodes.by: First stated by Helge Tverberg, 1966
nodes.note: The case r = 2 was proved earlier by Radon and is known as Radon's theorem. A topological version with continuous maps holds when r is a prime power but has counterexamples for other r.

nodes.name: Baranyai's theorem
nodes.statement: Let 2 ≤ r < k be integers with r dividing k. Then the r-element subsets of a k-element set can be split into C(k−1, r−1) groups, each group being a partition of the k elements into subsets of size r, so that every r-element subset appears in exactly one group.
nodes.by: Zsolt Baranyai, 1975; the case r = 3 was established by R. Peltesohn in 1936
nodes.note: The case r = 2 says that the edges of a complete graph with an even number of vertices split into perfect matchings. That case can be used to schedule round-robin tournaments.

nodes.name: Veblen's theorem
nodes.statement: The set of edges of a finite graph can be written as a union of disjoint simple cycles if and only if every vertex has even degree.
nodes.by: Introduced by Veblen, 1912
nodes.note: It is closely related to Euler's theorem of 1736 on Euler tours. Unlike that theorem, it also applies to disconnected graphs, and it can be generalized to infinite graphs in which every vertex has finite degree.

nodes.name: Vizing's conjecture
nodes.statement: For any graphs G and H, the domination number of the Cartesian product of G and H is at least the product of the domination numbers of G and H: γ(G □ H) ≥ γ(G)γ(H).
nodes.by: Vizing, 1968
nodes.note: It is known to hold when either graph has domination number one, for cycles, and for graphs with domination number two. Clark and Suen (2000) proved that the domination number of the product is at least half the conjectured bound.

nodes.name: Theorem on friends and strangers
nodes.statement: Call two people mutual strangers if they have not met before and mutual acquaintances if they have. In any party of six people, there are at least three who are all pairwise mutual strangers or all pairwise mutual acquaintances.
nodes.by: A simple case of the general theorem proved by Frank Ramsey, 1930
nodes.note: Six is the smallest party size for which this holds: five people can be arranged so that no three are all strangers or all acquaintances. In Ramsey theory this is written R(3,3:2) = 6.

nodes.name: Kuratowski's theorem
nodes.statement: A finite graph can be drawn in the plane without edges crossing if and only if it does not contain a subgraph that is a subdivision of K₅ (the complete graph on five vertices) or of K₃,₃ (the complete bipartite graph with three vertices on each side). A subdivision is obtained by replacing edges with paths.
nodes.by: Kazimierz Kuratowski, 1930; independently proved by Orrin Frink and Paul Smith in 1930, though their proof was never published; reportedly also proved by Lev Pontryagin around 1927, unpublished
nodes.note: It is a forbidden graph characterization of planar graphs. It is equivalent to Wagner's theorem, which uses minors of the same two graphs.

nodes.name: Cereceda's conjecture
nodes.statement: Let G be a graph with n vertices and degeneracy at most d. Then any two colorings of G with at most d + 2 colors can be turned into each other by changing the color of one vertex at a time, staying within colorings with at most d + 2 colors, using a number of steps that is O(n²), that is at most a constant times n².
nodes.by: Posed as a question by Luis Cereceda in his 2007 doctoral dissertation; known as Cereceda's conjecture by 2018
nodes.note: If true, it would be best possible, as the space of 3-colorings of a path graph has quadratic diameter. It is known that the diameter is polynomial for every fixed d.

nodes.name: Hypergraph removal lemma
nodes.statement: Let H be an r-uniform hypergraph (every edge joins exactly r vertices) with h vertices. For every ε > 0 there is a δ > 0 such that any r-uniform hypergraph G on n vertices with fewer than δnʰ subhypergraphs isomorphic to H can be made free of copies of H by removing at most εnʳ edges.
nodes.by: First proved by Nagle, Rödl, Schacht and Skokan and, independently, by Gowers
nodes.note: It generalizes the graph removal lemma (the case r = 2) and can be used to prove Szemerédi's theorem.

nodes.name: Kotzig's theorem
nodes.statement: Every polyhedral graph (the graph of the vertices and edges of a convex polyhedron) has an edge whose two endpoints have total degree at most 13. Equivalently, every convex polyhedron has two adjacent faces with a total of at most 13 sides.
nodes.by: Anton Kotzig, 1955, in the dual form about faces; named and popularized in the west by Branko Grünbaum in the 1970s
nodes.note: The triakis icosahedron is an extreme case, where no edge has smaller total degree. The theorem does not extend to all planar graphs.

nodes.name: Cayley's formula
nodes.statement: For every positive integer n, the number of trees on n labeled vertices is n^(n−2). Equivalently, a complete graph on n labeled vertices has n^(n−2) spanning trees.
nodes.by: First discovered by Carl Wilhelm Borchardt in 1860 and proved via a determinant; Arthur Cayley extended it in 1889
nodes.note: Many proofs are known, including ones using Kirchhoff's matrix tree theorem and Prüfer sequences.

nodes.name: Szpilrajn extension theorem
nodes.statement: Every partial order on a set is contained in a total order on that set. A partial order is a relation that is reflexive, transitive and antisymmetric. A total order is a partial order in which any two elements are comparable.
nodes.by: Edward Szpilrajn, 1930
nodes.note: The proof uses the axiom of choice in the form of Zorn's lemma, and some form of the axiom of choice is necessary to prove the theorem.

nodes.name: Kőnig's theorem
nodes.statement: In any bipartite graph, the number of edges in a maximum matching equals the number of vertices in a minimum vertex cover.
nodes.by: Dénes Kőnig, 1931; discovered independently in 1931 by Jenő Egerváry in the more general case of weighted graphs
nodes.note: For graphs that are not bipartite, the minimum vertex cover may be larger than the maximum matching. The theorem lets minimum vertex covers of bipartite graphs be computed efficiently.

nodes.name: Menger's theorem
nodes.statement: Let G be a finite undirected graph and x and y two distinct vertices. Then the minimum number of edges whose removal disconnects x and y equals the maximum number of pairwise edge-disjoint paths from x to y.
nodes.by: Karl Menger, 1927
nodes.note: This is the edge-connectivity version. It implies that a graph is k-edge-connected if and only if every pair of vertices has k edge-disjoint paths between them.

nodes.name: Handshaking lemma
nodes.statement: In every finite undirected graph, the number of vertices of odd degree is even. Here the degree of a vertex is the number of edges touching it, with a loop counted twice; equivalently, the sum of all degrees equals twice the number of edges.
nodes.by: Leonhard Euler, 1736
nodes.note: Euler proved it in his paper on the Seven Bridges of Königsberg. It does not hold in its usual form for infinite graphs.

nodes.name: Lovász conjecture
nodes.statement: Every finite connected vertex-transitive graph contains a Hamiltonian path.
nodes.by: László Lovász, 1969 (he originally stated the problem in the opposite way)
nodes.note: In 1996 László Babai published a conjecture sharply contradicting this one, and both conjectures remain widely open.

nodes.name: Proizvolov's identity
nodes.statement: Split the numbers 1, 2, …, 2N into two subsets of N numbers each. List one subset in increasing order A₁ < … < A_N and the other in decreasing order B₁ > … > B_N. Then |A₁ − B₁| + |A₂ − B₂| + … + |A_N − B_N| = N².
nodes.by: Posed by Vyacheslav Proizvolov as a problem in the 1985 All-Union Soviet Student Olympiads
nodes.note: The identity concerns sums of differences of positive integers.

nodes.name: Dushnik–Miller theorem
nodes.statement: Every countably infinite linear order has an order embedding into itself other than the identity.
nodes.by: Ben Dushnik and E. W. Miller, 1940
nodes.note: The same paper shows, using the axiom of choice, that the statement does not always hold for uncountable linear orders. In reverse mathematics the theorem for countable linear orders has the same strength as ACA_0.

nodes.name: Erdős–Dushnik–Miller theorem
nodes.statement: Every infinite graph contains either a countably infinite independent set, or a clique with the same cardinality as the whole graph.
nodes.by: First published by Miller, 1941; the paper credited Paul Erdős with assistance in the proof
nodes.note: An equivalent complementary form says every infinite graph contains either a countably infinite clique or an independent set of the same cardinality as the whole graph.

nodes.name: Laver's theorem
nodes.statement: Order embeddability of countable total orders is a well-quasi-ordering. That is, in every infinite sequence of countable totally ordered sets, there is an order embedding from an earlier member of the sequence into a later one.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Roland Fraïssé, 1948; proved by Richard Laver, 1971
nodes.note: Laver also proved the same result for countable unions of scattered orders. In reverse mathematics its strength lies between ATR₀ and Π¹₁-CA₀, it is weaker than Π¹₁-CA₀, and it is open whether it is equivalent to ATR₀.

nodes.name: Graham–Pollak theorem
nodes.statement: The edges of a complete graph on n vertices cannot be partitioned into fewer than n−1 complete bipartite graphs.
nodes.by: Ronald Graham and Henry O. Pollak, 1971 and 1972, crediting Hans Witsenhausen for a key lemma
nodes.note: A partition into exactly n−1 complete bipartite graphs exists, for example using stars. Aigner and Ziegler write that all known proofs rest on linear algebra and no combinatorial proof is known.

nodes.name: Ryser's conjecture
nodes.statement: If a hypergraph H is r-partite, meaning its vertices can be split into r sets so that every edge contains exactly one vertex from each set, then its smallest transversal size τ(H) is at most r − 1 times its largest matching size ν(H): τ(H) ≤ (r − 1)·ν(H).
nodes.by: First appeared in the Ph.D. thesis of J. R. Henderson, 1971, whose advisor was Herbert John Ryser
nodes.note: The case r = 2 follows from Kőnig's theorem, and the case r = 3 was proved by Ron Aharoni. Truncated projective planes show that the factor r − 1 cannot be made smaller.

nodes.name: Erdős–Szekeres theorem
nodes.statement: Given r and s, every sequence of distinct real numbers of length at least (r−1)(s−1)+1 contains an increasing subsequence of length r or a decreasing subsequence of length s.
nodes.by: Paul Erdős and George Szekeres, 1935
nodes.note: It is a finitary result that makes precise one of the corollaries of Ramsey's theorem.
